title: Longest Well-Formed Bracket Stretch
statement:
The string s contains only '(' and ')'. A stretch is well-formed if every opening bracket in it is closed later in the same stretch and no closing bracket appears without an opener before it, like "(())()".

Return the length of the longest contiguous substring of s that is well-formed. Return 0 if there is none.

examples.why: The middle "(()())" is well-formed. The stray ")" at the start and "(" at the end cannot join it.
There are two matched pairs, but the unmatched "(" in between splits them. Counting all matched pairs would wrongly give 4.
"()" followed directly by "(())" joins into one well-formed stretch of length 6.

hints: For one fixed start, you can walk right with a balance counter. When is the stretch from that start well-formed, and when can you stop?
A well-formed stretch can never cross an unmatched ')' or an unmatched '('. Those unmatched positions split the string into pieces.

Keep a stack of indexes, starting with -1 as a floor. Push the index of every '('. On ')', pop; if the stack is now empty, push this index as the new floor, else the stretch ending here has length i − top of stack.

explain.intuition:
Match brackets the usual way, with a stack of indexes of open '('. The brackets that never get matched act as walls: no well-formed stretch can contain one. Between two walls, everything is matched, and that whole gap is well-formed.

The trick is to keep the most recent wall on the stack too. Start with -1 as an imaginary wall before the string. When a ')' pops its partner, the new top of the stack is the nearest position that is still open or a wall, so the stretch ending at i runs from just after that top to i. When a ')' finds nothing to pop, it is itself a wall: it becomes the new floor.
steps: For ')', pop. If the stack is now empty, push i as the new floor.
Otherwise set best = max(best, i − top), where top is the current top of the stack.
pitfalls: Counting matched pairs over the whole string. Pairs separated by an unmatched bracket do not form one stretch.
Measuring from the matching '(' instead of from the top of the stack. In "()(())" that misses that the first pair joins the second.
A single left-to-right counter pass: it cannot see "(()", where the balance never returns to zero. You need a second pass from the right, or the stack.

complexity.space: O(n), or O(1) with the two-pass counter

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: From each start, walk right with a balance counter. A zero balance marks a well-formed stretch; a negative one means stop.

solutions.title: Stack of indexes with a floor
solutions.idea: The stack holds open '(' positions on top of the last unmatched position. After a match, the distance to the stack top is the stretch length.

solutions.title: Two counter passes
solutions.idea: Left to right, count opens and closes; equal counts mark a stretch, more closes resets. The mirror pass from the right catches stretches with extra '(' before them.

followups: Solve it with a DP where dp[i] is the longest well-formed stretch ending at i. What does a ')' at i look back at?
Return the start index of the longest stretch as well. Which version makes that easiest?
